result:
The morning light hits my desk differently in October, slanting through the blinds with a golden weight that feels almost tangible. I've been thinking about how we measure time—calendars, clocks, the slow accumulation of coffee rings on paper—and how inadequate all of it feels against the actual experience of living.

Last week I found a photograph of my grandmother at twenty-three, standing on a pier in Maine. She's laughing at something off-camera, wind-whipped hair, holding a pair of shoes rather than wearing them. The image arrested me because I realized I'd been thinking of her as *old* my entire life. She was old when I was born, old when she died, old in every story my father told. But here was youth, possibility, the same uncertainty I feel now pressing against my own ribs. She didn't know yet about the three children, the divorce, the small house in Ohio where she'd spend decades, the cancer that would take her in a February no one expected.

We contain multitudes backward and forward, I suppose. The child I was at seven still exists in the way I flinch at loud noises, the way I can't sleep without some small light burning. The old woman I might become already lurks in my morning stiffness, my sudden preference for early nights, my growing intolerance for loud restaurants.

What strikes me is the loneliness of it. Not sad loneliness, but the solitude of being the only witness to your own continuity. I can tell you about that seven-year-old, but I cannot *show* you. The photograph of my grandmother comes close, but it's still a door slightly ajar, not a room you can enter.

Maybe that's why we write.
